title: Sell Mineral Rights in Midland County, TX/NM
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Midland County, TX
metaDescription: Midland County is the operational heart of the basin, home to the Spraberry Trend and the operators who drill it. We buy mineral and royalty interests here directly.
heroLead: Midland County is where most of the companies drilling the rest of the basin keep their offices, and that changes how mineral interests here get bought and sold.
intro: I spent a good stretch of my career in Midland, and if you own minerals in this county you're sitting under one of the most studied pieces of rock in American oil and gas history. The Spraberry Trend was discovered here in 1949 and turned out to be one of the largest oil fields by surface area in the country, and decades later the same acreage got a second life once operators figured out how to landing horizontal wells in the Wolfcamp benches underneath it.

That long history is exactly why Midland County mineral ownership gets complicated. You might have an interest tracing back to a 1950s vertical lease that's been assigned, re-assigned, and split among heirs three or four times since, sitting under a section that now has modern horizontal wells stacked on top of the old vertical bores. We sort out which production you're actually entitled to before we quote anything.

sections.heading: Stacked pay changes how your interest should be valued
paragraphs: Midland County acreage typically has several productive intervals stacked on top of each other, the Spraberry itself along with the Wolfcamp A, B, and lower benches, sometimes the Dean and Jo Mill zones too. A tract that looks unremarkable based on one old vertical well might have three or four modern horizontal wells targeting different depths beneath it, each with its own spacing unit and division order.

This is where a lot of owners get shortchanged by buyers who price off a single well rather than checking every zone. We pull the full wellbore history against your tract across all producing intervals rather than whichever single well happens to be paying you right now.

sections.heading: Being close to headquarters cuts both ways
paragraphs: Because so many operators are headquartered in Midland, permitting and development activity here tends to be well documented and fast-moving, which is good for owners wanting current information about their acreage. It also means Midland County land and mineral prices get more attention and more competing buyers than a lot of surrounding counties.

That's a point in your favor as a seller, but it also means it pays to get more than one number before deciding. We'll show you our reasoning, based on your specific production history and nearby permits, so you can judge our offer against anything else you've received.

sections.heading: Urban growth and mineral estates
paragraphs: Midland itself has grown enough that some mineral tracts in the county now sit under developed residential or commercial surface. That doesn't change your mineral ownership, Texas law keeps the mineral and surface estates separate, but it can affect access for future drilling on some of the more built-up sections near town.

If your family's minerals came down through a ranching or farming operation that predates the city's growth, we're used to reconstructing that history from courthouse deed records even when the current surface bears no resemblance to what it looked like when the mineral reservation was first made.

faqs.question: How do you value a tract with multiple stacked pay zones?
faqs.answer: We pull the full production and permit history for every interval under your tract instead of only the well currently paying you, since Midland County acreage commonly has several productive zones like the Spraberry and multiple Wolfcamp benches stacked beneath one surface location.

faqs.question: Does it matter that operators are headquartered in Midland?
faqs.answer: It generally means more documented, faster-moving activity and more competing buyers for acreage here, which can work in your favor. We encourage owners to compare offers before deciding.

faqs.question: My minerals are under a developed part of Midland now. Can they still be sold?
faqs.answer: Yes. Surface development doesn't change mineral ownership under Texas law, though it can affect future drilling access on some built-up sections. We'll flag anything relevant to your specific tract.

faqs.question: My family's lease dates back to the 1950s Spraberry discovery era. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: Not for us. We regularly trace chain of title through decades of assignments and heirship on older Midland County leases using county clerk deed records.

faqs.question: How quickly can a Midland County sale close?
faqs.answer: With clean title and a current division order, most Midland County purchases close within two to four weeks. Interests needing probate or title curative work take longer, and we'll give you a realistic timeline upfront.

faqs.question: Why do I keep getting offer letters from different buyers for my Midland County interest?
faqs.answer: Given how much documented activity and headquarters presence this county has, it draws more buyer competition than most surrounding counties. That's a reason to compare offers rather than accept the first one, and we're comfortable having our number reviewed against others.

faqs.question: Do you buy interests still tied to the original 1949 Spraberry discovery wells?
faqs.answer: Yes, though most of those original wellbores have long since been replaced or supplemented by later development. We trace the full history from the original lease forward to whatever is currently producing on your tract.
